questions.q: In a light clock, the time \(t_0\) for a pulse of light to pass from mirror A to mirror B and back, measured in the frame of reference in which the clock is at rest, is defined as which quantity?
options: The Lorentz factor of the clock
One tick of the clock
The dilated time of the clock
The proper length of the clock
questions.explanation: With the mirror separation \(L\), the round-trip time \(t_0 = 2L/c\) is defined to be one tick of the clock. In the clock's own rest frame the two events bracketing a tick (the pulse leaving A and returning to A) happen at the same point in space, which is why \(t_0\) is the proper time.

questions.q: What is the proper time \(t_0\) in special relativity?
options: The time measured in a frame of reference where the two events occur at the same points in space
The longer time measured by an observer who sees the clock moving
The time measured using two separate clocks at different points in space
The time light takes to cross the universe at speed c
questions.explanation: The proper time \(t_0\) is the time measured in the frame of reference where the two events occur at the same points in space — the clock's own frame. Because gamma is always greater than 1, the dilated time \(t = t_0\gamma\) is always greater than \(t_0\), hence the term 'time dilation'.

questions.q: From memory: state the key property of the Lorentz factor gamma, and explain what it implies about the dilated time \(t\) compared with the proper time \(t_0\).
keyPoints: Gamma is always greater than 1 (it equals 1 only when v = 0).
Because gamma is greater than 1, the dilated time t is always greater than the proper time t0 — hence the term 'time dilation'.
As v approaches c the value under the square root approaches 0, so gamma climbs without limit.
questions.explanation: From the time dilation formula \(t = t_0\gamma\), the fact that gamma is never less than 1 is your error-checker: a moving clock's measured tick is always longer than its proper (rest-frame) tick. If you recalled 'gamma is greater than 1, so t is greater than t0', grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: James observes a clock held by his friend Mabry moving past at 0.5c. He notices the hands change from 12 pm to 12.05 pm, indicating that 5 minutes have passed for the clock. How much time has passed for James?
questions.given: \(v = 0.5c\),  proper time \(t_0 = 5\) minutes (the two events occur at the same place on Mabry's clock)
questions.explanation: Identify the proper time first: Mabry's clock is present at both events, so 5 minutes is the proper time (the short one). Then gamma at 0.5c is 1.155, and \(t = t_0\gamma = 5.775\) minutes. The moving clock is measured to run slow.

questions.q: Mabry travels past James at 0.5c, and James sees Mabry's clock running slow. What does Mabry observe about James's clock?
options: She sees James's clock running fast, to balance out the effect
She sees James's clock keeping the same time as her own
She sees James's clock running slow by the same factor, because the situations are symmetrical
She sees James's clock stop entirely
questions.explanation: These situations are symmetrical: Mabry sees James moving at 0.5c, and James sees Mabry moving at 0.5c, so each measures the other's clock running slow by exactly the same factor. There is no contradiction because they do not agree on which events are simultaneous.

questions.q: Observers on Earth observe the length of a spacecraft travelling at 0.5c to have contracted. To what percentage of its proper length is the spacecraft contracted according to the observers?
working: So the spacecraft is measured at 86.6% of its proper length — a contraction of 13.4%.
questions.explanation: Length contracts, so you divide the proper length by gamma: \(L = L_0/\gamma\). At 0.5c, gamma is 1.155, giving 0.866, i.e. 86.6% of the proper length (a 13.4% contraction). Never multiply a length by gamma — that would make it longer, which is the classic mark-destroying slip.

questions.q: According to the Lorentz contraction, a spaceship moving at relativistic speed is measured as shorter. Which of its dimensions are affected?
options: All dimensions contract uniformly by the factor gamma
Only the length along the direction of motion is contracted; the other dimensions are not affected
Only the dimensions perpendicular to the motion contract
The width and height contract but the length stays the same
questions.explanation: The Lorentz contraction \(L = L_0/\gamma\) is the shortening of an object along its direction of motion when measured from a frame moving relative to it. This change in length applies only to the dimension along the direction of motion; the other dimensions are not affected. The proper length \(L_0\) is the length measured in the object's rest frame.

questions.q: In the Rossi-Hall experiment, muons produced in the upper atmosphere have a laboratory half-life of 1.56 microseconds, yet far more survive the journey to the ground than expected. From the Earth's frame, why?
options: The muons travel faster than light to outrun their decay
The muons are so numerous that some always survive by chance
The muons travel so fast that their decay is time-dilated, decaying at a much slower rate for observers on Earth
The atmosphere slows the muons so they live longer
questions.explanation: Bruno Rossi and David Hall (1941) found far more muons survived than predicted without time dilation. Travelling near light speed relative to Earth, the muons decayed at a much slower rate for Earth observers: the journey took about 6.5 microseconds on Earth clocks, but the muons decayed as though only about 0.7 microseconds had passed. From the muon's own frame, length contraction shrinks the atmosphere to a small hill instead.

questions.q: Describe the 1971 Hafele-Keating experiment and what it showed about time dilation.
keyPoints: Atomic clocks were flown on commercial airliners and compared with an identical clock that remained on the ground.
The flown clocks recorded different amounts of time, agreeing with Einstein's prediction of time dilation.
The reference frames were not strictly inertial (the clocks circled the Earth under gravity), so the result combines special and general relativity.
questions.explanation: Hafele-Keating flew precise caesium atomic clocks around the world and found the flown clocks disagreed with the ground clock by the amount relativity predicts. Treat it as confirmation that time dilation is real, but note it does not isolate special relativity alone because gravity (general relativity) also plays a role.

questions.q: A question asks you to account for time dilation using the light-clock thought experiment. Which sentence is the specific mark-earning idea the marker is looking for?
options: The light speeds up to cover the longer diagonal, so the tick is unchanged
The pulse follows a longer diagonal path but must still travel at the constant speed of light, so each tick takes longer for the external observer
The mirrors move apart, so the pulse has further to travel and slows down
The clock physically breaks when it moves, so it ticks slowly
questions.explanation: By postulate two the pulse cannot pick up the spaceship's sideways speed — it must still travel at the constant speed of light. A longer diagonal path covered at the same speed must take more time, so each tick takes longer as measured from the external frame. The clause 'must still travel at the speed of light' is the mark.

questions.q: Explain how observations of cosmic-origin muons at the Earth's surface provide evidence for special relativity. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Muons are created high in the atmosphere and travel toward the ground at close to the speed of light, but their half-life is so short that, classically, almost all should decay before reaching the surface. In fact far more are detected at sea level than classical physics predicts. From the Earth's frame, the muon's high speed means its internal clock is time-dilated, so its decay time is lengthened by the Lorentz factor and it survives long enough to reach the ground. From the muon's own frame, its half-life is normal, but the atmosphere is length-contracted along the direction of motion, so the distance to be travelled is greatly shortened, allowing it to reach the ground before decaying. Both frames independently predict that many more muons survive, in agreement with observation.

criteria.descriptor: States that classically almost all muons should decay before reaching the ground, yet far more are detected than predicted.
Earth frame: the muon's clock is time-dilated, lengthening its decay time so it reaches the ground.
Muon frame: the atmosphere is length-contracted along the direction of motion, shortening the journey.
Concludes both frames give the same result, matching the observed muon count.

questions.explanation: A full-mark answer must give both frames: Earth frame uses time dilation, muon frame uses length contraction, and both reach the identical conclusion. Giving only one frame caps your marks.
